canberra.title: No separate inquiry into Brindabella car park as committee warns of ‘concerning precedent’
canberra.snippet: Brindabella Christian College’s controversial carpark will be examined as part of a wider probe into planning enforcement, as an ACT Legi...
canberra.content:
22 September 2026

Start the conversation

Brindabella Christian College carpark is one of seven sites under scrutiny. Photo: Region.

Brindabella Christian College’s controversial carpark will be examined as part of a wider probe into planning enforcement, as an ACT Legislative Assembly committee warned that creating a pathway for its approval could set a “concerning precedent” and appear to reward non-compliance.

The Standing Committee on Environment and Planning confirmed on Tuesday (22 September) that it would scrutinise government enforcement at the Lyneham site through its broader inquiry into controlled activity orders, rather than hold a separate investigation into Draft Major Plan Amendment 12 (DPA-12).

Committee chair Jo Clay told the Assembly the wider inquiry would examine “whether there are broader systemic issues relating to the effectiveness of controlled activity order provisions and government enforcement of lease conditions, ensuring maintenance of facilities, compliance with Crown leases, and preventing unauthorised developments”.

The Brindabella carpark is one of seven sites specifically identified for examination, alongside Big Splash Waterpark, Hawker Tennis Centre, Gungahlin Cinema, Phillip Swimming Pool and Ice-Skating Centre, the Manuka Hotel site and Richardson shops.

DPA-12 was referred to the committee on 22 July, but it resolved on 12 August not to conduct a separate inquiry into the amendment.

Ms Clay said the circumstances surrounding the carpark had already received extensive consideration through the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT) and ongoing court proceedings, while the broader inquiry would examine the enforcement issues raised by the case.

“The committee notes that any decision on DPA 12 could be superseded by future court decisions and has urged the minister to take caution in taking any steps before a final outcome is reached in the courts,” she said.

The committee concluded a separate inquiry into DPA-12 would be unlikely to add materially to the scrutiny already occurring through the courts, planning system and its wider investigation.

But it issued a strong warning about what could happen if the amendment was approved.

DPA-12 would allow a carpark to be assessed on the site despite its current PRZ1 Urban Open Space zoning. It would not approve or regularise the existing carpark, and any future proposal would still need to go through a development application process, considering issues such as traffic, safety, design and environmental impacts.

“Approving DPA 12 would act as a concerning precedent which in effect retrospectively approves the unapproved development of public unleased land,” Ms Clay said on behalf of the committee.

“It could send a signal that the ACT Government tolerates and rewards non-compliance with lease conditions and the planning system.”

The dispute stretches back years. The college sealed the public land adjoining its Lyneham campus for use as a carpark in 2016 without development approval. In 2023, ACAT found the carpark was not appropriately zoned and lacked development approval, later ordering it closed and requiring the site to be restored if the college could not secure the necessary approvals.

However, in February 2024, the ACT Supreme Court granted a stay of those orders, allowing the carpark to remain open while the college’s appeal is determined.

canberra.title: Hanson dodges media after ‘don’t give up’ speech to huge crowd of supporters at Henty
canberra.snippet: One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has implored farmers to tell their kids to “hang in there”, promising change is on the horiz...
canberra.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson was swamped by legions of fans, both young and old, at the 2026 Henty Machinery Field Days on Tuesday. Photo: Jodie O’Sullivan.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has implored farmers to tell their kids to “hang in there”, promising change is on the horizon during Tuesday’s official opening of the 2026 Henty Machinery Field Days.

The crowd gave Senator Hanson a rousing reception as she ascended the steps at The Stump to address a packed crowd, but journalists were later left in the lurch after a scheduled media appearance failed to materialise.

The 72-year-old politician said Australia needed productive farms, growing businesses and towns where young people could get a trade, find a job, buy a home and raise a family.

“But what I’m hearing now is farmers saying to their kids, there’s no future in farming,” Senator Hanson said.

“I don’t want you telling your kids that anymore. I want you to tell them to hang in there because change is coming and I know it’s coming.

“I want you to stay here on the farms. I want you to produce the food for this nation. Do not give up. I have not given up.”

It was a message warmly received by a crowd Senator Hanson clearly enjoyed addressing.

“This time last week I was Parliament House. You know I’d rather be right here,” she told them.

“You are the beating heart of this nation, so it’s great to see so many people.”

The controversial politician’s arrival in a distinctive orange hat drew an immediate flurry of fans – young and old – around her.

Her appearance also came on the back of a fresh controversy over a Channel Nine interview with Ku Klux Klan leader Thomas Robb, who praised Senator Hanson’s immigration views – a link she has angrily rejected.

Flanked by security at Henty, her minders and with federal MP Barnaby Joyce and newly elected Farrer MP David Farley in tow, Senator Hanson appeared more than happy to pose for photographs, sign hats and chat.

But while Senator Hanson lined up to meet a seemingly endless procession of supporters, journalists hoping to question the One Nation leader were afforded no such opportunity.

A scheduled 11:30 am media stand-up did not proceed, leaving television crews and reporters waiting outside a private luncheon.

Senator Hanson subsequently left through a rear exit before making her way across the field days site for the NSW Farmers’ Pollies in the Paddock forum.

There, it was back to selfies with a loyal legion of fans.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson officially opens the 2026 Henty Machinery Field Days. Photo: Toby Kohlhagen.

With a record 896 exhibitors, this year’s event marks 50 years at its permanent location on Cookardinia Road, Henty.

But trademark highlights, including the announcement of the coveted Machine of the Year award, were somewhat overshadowed by the political personalities present.

At times, the reception had more of the flavour of a visiting celebrity than a politician. However, Joyce and Farley were notably more amenable to questions from reporters on the ground.

Senator Hanson’s reluctance to face the media came on a day she was also embroiled in national controversy after Nine aired an interview with US Ku Klux Klan leader Thomas Robb, who expressed support for aspects of her immigration stance.

The Senator has emphatically rejected any association between One Nation and the white supremacist organisation, describing such a link as “absurd and offensive”.

Immigration nevertheless featured prominently in her Henty address.

Senator Hanson used the agricultural labour needs of farmers to defend One Nation’s recently announced immigration policy, rejecting suggestions it would prevent farms from accessing overseas workers.

“Now there’s been a lot of lies spread around that we want to stop the workers coming in. That is not part of my plan,” she said.

“We are going to, our immigration policy will support and does support PALM (Pacific Australia Labour Mobility) workers, seasonal workers, those skilled workers and backpackers. We are not putting any limit on that.

“What we are doing is stopping those family members of students and those people coming to this country don’t need to be here.”

Agricultural labour was, she said, one area where government policy had to recognise the realities outside the nation’s capital.

“Agriculture depends on reliable seasonal labour,” she said. “Harvest does not wait for Canberra.”

Water also featured heavily.

“Here in the Riverina, water means production, it means jobs, it means businesses and families staying on their farms,” Senator Hanson said.

“Healthy rivers matter, so do healthy communities and productive farms.”

She singled out Mr Farley’s advocacy on the issue, saying she was “so proud” to have him representing Farrer and that he had been “pushing the issue constantly” since entering parliament.

There was no shortage of One Nation supporters in attendance on day one of the field days. Photo: Jodie O’Sullivan.

For his part, the newly elected Farrer MP used his address to paint a broader picture of the economic challenges confronting the country.

Mr Farley told the crowd Australia was carrying $1.1 trillion in debt and argued increased production and capacity were essential to tackling it.

“We have to earn our way out of it,” he said.

His assertion that people coming to Australia needed to contribute drew one of the louder responses of the morning.

“We don’t have room for passengers,” Mr Farley said, to further rounds of applause.

The pair’s appearances came after debate surrounding HMFD’s decision to invite Senator Hanson to open the event.

On Tuesday, however, there was little sign of hostility around The Stump.

And after all the talk of politics, immigration, water and cost pressures came something altogether more practical.

“I’m looking forward to getting around, seeing the venues, having a look at the machinery,” she said.

And apparently she wasn’t merely window shopping: “I am looking for a tractor. I have got my own property …”

After almost three decades of “water under the bridge”, Senator Hanson returned to Henty with plenty to say from the stage and no shortage of faithful wanting her attention.

Whether she found the tractor she was looking for remained to be seen.

The waiting media, however, were rather unceremoniously left empty-handed.

Original Article published by Jodie O’Sullivan on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Apple hit with $18,000 compo bill over city store’s accessible toilet
canberra.snippet: Apple has been ordered to pay a former employee at its Canberra city store $18,000 in compensation for indirect discrimination because th...
canberra.content:
ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal found the employee had been disadvantaged. Photo: Albert McKnight.

Apple has been ordered to pay a former employee at its Canberra city store $18,000 in compensation for indirect discrimination because the accessible toilet was used as a storeroom.

The employee had a physical condition due to several operations which required him to suddenly go to the toilet about 10 times a day.

He was on staff from September 2019 until March 2024, although from October 2021 he took leave and did not return to work, resigning in March 2024.

The employee took Apple to the ACT Human Rights Commission in June 2024, which referred the complaint to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal, claiming disability discrimination under the Discrimination Act 1991.

The main issue was the employee’s difficulty using the accessible toilet, which stored cleaning materials and a large floor cleaner, with a cleaning cupboard behind it, and the store’s delay in rectifying the situation.

He said that a few weeks after he started work with the Apple store, he told supervisor Janine Healy about his health needs, how cleaning items prevented the accessible toilet door from closing, and that staff also used the accessible toilet as a changing area.

He told her the cleaning products needed to be removed from the accessible toilet, and that the accessible toilet should be reserved for people with disabilities rather than general staff or those using it as a change room.

Some equipment was removed, but cleaning supplies and equipment, including the large cleaning machine, remained.

“I continued to use the accessible toilet; however, I was heavily restricted in my movements in the toilet due to the large cleaning machine, which prevented my safe and ready access to the facility,” the employee said.

He also had to wait to use the general staff toilets, although Senior Member Robert Orr found he did not have to wait as long as he claimed.

On 1 July 2021, the employee suffered a hand injury using the accessible toilet when attempting to reach the towel dispenser that was obstructed by the cleaning machine.

He again told Ms Healy that the accessible toilet should not be used as a storeroom and that he needed full, unobstructed access to the toilet due to his health concerns, raising the issue of the floor cleaner in particular.

But he was told that there was nowhere else to store the cleaning materials and equipment.

By September 2023, the equipment and the floor cleaner had been moved out of the accessible bathroom, and by 2024 a store renovation meant there were three bathrooms: one accessible at the back of the store, and two elsewhere, none used for storage.

Mr Orr could not find a claim of direct discrimination, which requires being treated unfavourably because of disability.

“When the applicant raised his concerns, some of these were addressed; others were not addressed at that time but this was for reasons unrelated to his disability; and they were addressed at a later date,” he found.

“In other ways staff at the store supported the applicant to manage his condition while working.”

But for indirect discrimination, a condition or requirement must disadvantage the applicant because of a disability, and it is up to the respondent to show that it isn’t unreasonable.

Mr Orr found that the accessible bathroom situation did disadvantage the applicant.

“The fact that notwithstanding these factors he could manage to use the accessible toilet, or another toilet, does not defeat the claim,” he said.

“The respondent did not show that the condition or requirement was reasonable in the circumstances.”

The applicant sought compensation for loss of earnings and psychological injury, saying that the respondent’s actions caused him hurt, humiliation and distress.

But these were denied.

Mr Orr said this was not a case of intentional, calculated or cruel discrimination.

“This was a case of indirect discrimination where the respondent put in place quickly those measures it could to address the applicant’s bathroom complaints, and in time addressed all his complaints, and generally sought to assist the applicant to manage his condition,” he said.

This meant the Tribunal could not order a significant amount of compensation. The Tribunal awarded $18,000 in compensation.

canberra.title: Dogfight over dachshund ends up in ACAT after owners separate
canberra.snippet: All dog owners love their pets to pieces. After all, they are family. So if a dog’s owners separate, deciding who gets to keep thei...
canberra.content:
22 September 2026

ACAT has dealt with a former de facto couple fighting over who would keep their pet dachshund (not pictured). Photo: James Watson.

All dog owners love their pets to pieces. After all, they are family.

So if a dog’s owners separate, deciding who gets to keep their beloved pet must be incredibly difficult.

In fact, a former de facto couple from Canberra went to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT) to resolve this dilemma.

Presidential Member Marcus Hassall, in his recently published decision, said a man and a woman started their relationship in 2022 before the man bought a male dachshund in October 2023 for $2150.

“[The dog] was much loved by both of the parties and in the material is referred to, at times, as a ‘son’ of [the man],” the presidential member said.

“[The] material indicates that he was treated as a member of their family.”

But the couple’s de facto relationship ended acrimoniously in January 2026.

After the separation, the dachshund stayed living with the woman. As a result, the man went to ACAT in March and applied to have the dog returned to him.

He filed the application as a simple civil action for the delivery of goods. Essentially, he argued that the cost of the dog meant it fell within the jurisdictional limit of the civil matters the tribunal could deal with.

However, the woman argued the tribunal did not have the jurisdiction to deal with his application as it was a matter that should go before the Family Court.

The tribunal agreed and dismissed the man’s application, but he appealed, and Presidential Member Hassall heard it earlier this year.

“It is well known that certain courts exercise exclusive jurisdiction in relation to family law matters, including proceedings for the distribution of property following the breakdown of a marriage,” the presidential member said.

“For some decades now, the Family Law Act has also dealt with the distribution of property following the breakdown of a de facto relationship.”

He said the man argued all the evidence pointed to him being the sole owner of the dachshund. The woman claimed that, regardless of who originally paid for the dog, she should be declared its owner moving forward.

Presidential Member Hassall ultimately found the original tribunal correct in determining that ACAT lacked jurisdiction to deal with matters of this type.

He said when it came to de facto relationships, there was “absolutely no doubt” the intent of the legislation was that only the Family Court had the power to make orders relating to companion animals.

The appeal was dismissed.

The names of the man, the woman and the dachshund have been legally suppressed.

canberra.title: PM joins in statement to UN calling for AI to be brought under control
canberra.snippet: Australia has joined more than 20 other nations in urgently calling for artificial intelligence to be reined in so it remains under human...
canberra.content:
More than 20 world leaders have called for stronger international guardrails for AI. Photo: iStock

Australia has joined more than 20 other nations in urgently calling for artificial intelligence to be reined in so it remains under human control.

On the eve of the United Nations General Assembly gathering in New York, a group of world leaders signed a statement calling for strong global guardrails on the emerging technology.

“The rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed,” the statement says.

“To realise AI’s potential, industry, governments and society must act now.

“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”

Anthony Albanese was among the signatories to the statement, which makes it clear that efforts to date to counter the risks posed by AI have failed.

He was joined by the leaders of Canada, Germany, Spain, Finland and the European Commission.

Others included Norway, Bahrain, Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Latvia, Moldova, the Netherlands, Singapore, South Africa, Türkiye, and the United Arab Emirates.

The Prime Minister said he played a key role in developing the statement with other leaders.

“Artificial intelligence has the potential to improve lives, to strengthen our economy and productivity, and to massively advance science and medical breakthroughs,” he told reporters in New York.

“But humans need to be in control of it. If it’s going to be successful, then we need to make sure that humans are at the centre of everything that occurs … Australia played a central role in the statement. I was in direct discussions with President Stubb [Finland President Alexander Stubb], and we continue to engage with our neighbours.

“This has been something that is discussed between leaders, just as it’s been discussed around lounge rooms, around boardrooms, and around universities and around society.

“We know that artificial intelligence will have a massive impact on the way that our lives and our work is conducted, and that’s why we need to make sure that humans are at the centre of it and that they’re in control.”

The statement also calls for AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols and for the UN to look at establishing an international institution to develop and regulate AI standards.

The move is a show of strength from middle powers, who are increasingly uniting to push for stronger adherence to international order and rules.

It was delivered as the UN General Assembly expects AI to be a big topic of debate, with fears it could get heated and some players might try to hijack the discussion.

It also comes as US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping prepare to meet at the White House on Thursday.

Both superpowers are racing for global AI dominance.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, however, has suggested the two countries might establish an alert system to communicate “national security” level AI incidents.

Back in Australia, the Greens have welcomed the statement but say it needs to be backed up with binding commitments and also better action at the local level.

Greens AI spokesperson David Shoebridge said the world must not stand still while the United States and China “recklessly push frontier AI development” ahead of the ability to limit and safeguard the technology.

“This is a welcome change in tone from the Prime Minister, but it’s years behind the community’s concerns, and it only comes after global tech bros voiced concerns about AI’s safety,” Senator Shoebridge said.

“The work to protect Australians from runaway AI needs to be more than a New York talking point.

“This statement needs to be backed up with funding a serious AI safety institute and concerted local and global action to agree on binding AI safeguards.

“For all the talk, there is still not a single legislative response from the Albanese Labor government on AI. Not one.”

australia.title: Using AI to ‘talk to animals’ might make us feel clever – but what, if anything, does it do for them?
australia.snippet: As animal behaviorists increasingly use AI in their research, they grapple with how to wield the technology responsibly I’m sitting in a ...
australia.content:
I’m sitting in a small boat in Shark Bay, Australia, eavesdropping on a conversation between some of Earth’s most intelligent beings. The motor is off, the turquoise sea is glassy, and Stephanie King and I are motionless, transfixed by the whistles, clicks and squeezy, whirring noises made by the dolphins swimming below us.

If anyone could tell me what these big-brained social mammals are saying, it would be her. Based at the University of Bristol, she co-leads Shark Bay Dolphin Research, one of the longest-running wild dolphin research projects in the world. She has spent thousands of hours watching and listening to this population.

Like most other animal behaviorists, King is increasingly integrating artificial intelligence into her research process. “If it’s used responsibly, AI can transform what we can do with the data we collect,” she says. But when I ask her if AI will someday allow us to “speak dolphin”, she stiffens a little. “I think we’re doing the animals a disservice by focusing on that question,” she says.

  • Dolphins communicate, navigate and find food using buzzes, pops, whistles and other acoustic signals. These sounds were recorded in Shark Bay, western Australia via an underwater microphone by Amy Martin for the podcast Threshold

The problem, King says, is not AI itself, but the narrative being built around it. She sees her field increasingly framed as a quest for an AI-assisted animal interpreter, with headlines declaring that we’ve almost “cracked the secret language” of various creatures or are about to “decode animals’ speech”. There are even cash prizes for breakthroughs, including the Coller Dolittle Challenge, which seeks an algorithm for communicating with non-human organisms.

“It’s a sexy topic,” King acknowledges, but in her view, fundamentally misguided. She believes the allure of tech dollars and media attention is priming the pump of research in some unhealthy ways – nudging scientists to make premature claims about AI-assisted findings, and encouraging them to describe their work in sensational terms. “They tend to be biasing themselves towards the most exciting discovery,” says King, which “misleads us to what we know about these animals”.

What we know, in many cases, is in fact very little. Take dolphins. “They’ve been studied for decades, but we’re still scratching the surface with what many of the sounds mean,” King says. Sound itself likely means something different to dolphins than it does to us. They can detect pitches far outside our range of hearing, they process acoustic information much faster than we do, and our sensory systems are wired differently in important ways.

For example, both humans and dolphins can echolate – or use sound to navigate – but dolphins process echolocation information in the part of the brain connected to touch, while for us, it’s more connected to vision. In other words, instead of “seeing” with sound, dolphins might be hear-feeling, or feel-hearing, their way through their watery world. Whatever that experience is, it may be fundamentally inaccessible to us – and it’s not something we can comprehend by plugging their whistles and squeaks into a large language model. “We need to appreciate that they have a complex communication system that we barely understand,” says King. She believes our focus should be learning about that system – piecing together what dolphin behavior and communication means to other dolphins – rather than trying to hack into it, and start a conversation.

  • These high-pitched whistles are a very important part of dolphins’ social communication. Mothers use them to keep in contact with their calves and some whistles are even used as individual identifiers, or name-like calls. Credit: Stephanie King, Shark Bay Dolphin Research

Elephant researcher Joyce Poole agrees. “I get quite exasperated by this goal of being able to talk to the animals,” she says. “I think it’s kind of gimmicky.” One of the world’s leading experts on African savanna elephants, Poole has spent decades observing the animals in the wild, building up a treasure trove of annotated field recordings of their vocalizations, movements and interactions. She’s convinced that there are many layers and nuances of elephant communication that we don’t yet understand, but, like King, she’s skeptical about the concept of inserting ourselves into their dialogues. “Just the basic ability to understand what they have to say and what they are thinking about – that’s enough for me,” she says. “I don’t need to interfere in their lives more than necessary.”

  • Joyce Poole has documented female elephants making these overlapping sounds when a musth male arrives in their group, looking to breed. She refers to the sounds as “Female Chorus Rumbles” and they may include snorts, trumpets and roars, as well as low-pitched rumbles. Credit: The Elephant Ethogram, ElephantVoices

At the same time, Poole believes making the inner lives of elephants more legible to humans could transform how we treat them. “I hope that by showing that they’re capable of a more sophisticated kind of communication that we gain them some respect from our fellow humans, and save a place for them in the world, together with their ecosystems and their other fellow travelers,” she says.

Poole’s hope is widely shared, and is likely one of the main reasons so many of us are prone to click on stories with headlines about how AI is going to help us talk to animals. As extinction numbers rise and biodiversity declines, we’re desperate for some good news. Humans are also inherently fascinated by other animals; we’ve been telling stories about listening to and learning from them for as long as we’ve walked the Earth. Our technologies have in many ways cut us off from the rest of the living world – could this be a case when a new tool helps us to better tune into and care for our planetmates?

“I do see AI as a potentially promising avenue for knowing more, and understanding better, non-human animal lives,” says César Rodríguez-Garavito, founding director of the More Than Human Life (Moth) program at NYU, a leading hub for research and discourse on the rights of nature. He thinks AI could help give animals a voice in the decisions that shape their lives.

“More and more researchers and practitioners are asking themselves, ‘Well, how do we bring in the voices of, say, the whales in the regulation of a marine-protected area,’” he says. It may sound far-fetched to us now, but Rodríguez-Garavito says attempts to bring non-human voices into the realms of law and policy are already under way in countries around the world. “I think that this is no longer a science fiction question,” he says. Of course, we don’t need AI to tell us that whales are being negatively impacted by noise, ship strikes, climate disruption and pollution, but perhaps if we heard a direct translation of them expressing pain from underwater seismic testing, or mourning the loss of a calf killed by a ship, we would be more likely to act.

“But I cannot speak about potential benefits without speaking about risks,” Rodríguez-Garavito says. “We have, as human beings, a very mixed track record, to put it gently, in using technologies.” That record tells us that we can’t simply deploy AI in the wild and see what happens; we need to think through the risks ahead of time. There’s the possibility of intentional harm, like using AI-powered tools to trick or coerce animals, perhaps moving them into areas where they’re easier to kill (“I mean, think of trophy hunters,” says Poole). But if the past predicts the future, the greatest threats are not a few people using a new technology with malicious intent, but a whole lot of us using it without thinking about – or choosing to care about – the consequences.

“The nightmare scenario is one where we interrupt their communications and their lives at will, just for our entertainment,” says Rodríguez-Garavito. It’s not hard to imagine whale-watching companies using AI to lure animals toward boats, for example, or visitors to Yellowstone national park using apps to provoke wolves to howl, elk to bugle, or bison to bellow, exhausting and confusing the animals. Technologies are not beholden to the intentions of their makers. A tool created with the sincere goal of enhancing our respect for animals could end up having the opposite effect by turning them into playthings that we can pester and control.

  • Researchers Stephanie King and Laura Palmer document the movements and behaviors of a group of dolphins in Shark Bay. Buzzes and whistles from the dolphins are being picked up by underwater microphones and played through a speaker on the boat. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

In an attempt to help steer the field away from these dark scenarios, the Moth program recently published the Pepp framework (prepare, engage, prevent and protect), a set of ethical guidelines for the use of non-human animal communication technologies. But if and how it will actually get put into practice is uncertain. Rodríguez-Garavito says this is a trickle-down effect of the larger absence of legal and ethical boundaries around AI development. “At this point, there is no international agreement on AI,” he says. “It is a free-for-all. I would be much less concerned if we had general principles on what can and cannot be done with AI. There’s nothing like that, and this is why we’re having to develop them from scratch based on what’s been done in other fields of legal practice.”

  • Credit: The Elephant Ethogram, ElephantVoices

Mickey Pardo, who works with Joyce Poole as a senior scientist at ElephantVoices, also sees potential benefits and risks of AI-assisted animal communication tools, but he also wonders if the speculation is a bit overblown on both sides. “Playbacks can be stressful for animals even without AI – when you’re just taking prerecorded sounds and playing them back – especially if you don’t know the context of those sounds,” he says. Maybe a more sophisticated AI version could add to that stress, but Pardo sees it more as turning up the dial on a problem we already have, versus opening an entirely new can of worms.

He also questions whether we’re focusing too much on possible harms from AI when there are so many other ways we negatively impact animals’ lives, including in research settings.

“The way that animals are treated in biomedical science is so incredibly horrific compared to anything that anybody’s doing in the field of animal communication,” he says. “Not that we shouldn’t be thinking about the ethical implications [of AI] ahead of time. I just worry that perhaps we’re sucking up too much oxygen worrying about a hypothetical ethical problem when there are many very real, present ethical problems that we’re essentially ignoring.”

This oxygen-sucking, mesmerizing effect of AI – the attention and money poured toward it, and the almost magical powers we’re willing to ascribe to it – also concerns marine mammal researcher Luke Rendell, based at the University of St Andrews. “There’s been this idea put about that AI is going to find something that we couldn’t,” he says. “It’s something of a confidence trick, I think.”

Rendell believes the AI hype has gotten way ahead of the science, and that the public is being led to believe that we know – or are about to know – much more than we actually do about animal communication. For example, Earth Species Project claims on their website that “with exponential advances in AI and Large Language Models, decoding animal communication is no longer a question of if – it’s when” and states that they have already found support for their hypothesis that “AI can decode the shared structures of language across the Tree of Life”.

  • King says AI can be a very helpful tool when used in the right ways, but spending time with the animals in their habitat is essential for understanding what their vocal communication means to them. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

This is the sort of framing that gives Rendell hives. Like Stephanie King, he believes pursuing a quest to reveal the “language” of animals is loaded with humancentric bias that could actually limit our understanding of their unique and wildly diverse ways of getting their messages across. He’s also concerned about long-term damage to his field when the Dr Dolittle machine fails to materialize.

The study of animal communication has attracted a fair number of charlatans over the years, leading to boom-and-bust cycles of funding and credibility. Rendell says he entered the field of cetacean communication “just as it was recovering from a 15-year hangover” from the work of John Lilly, whose efforts to teach dolphins English using controversial methods – like giving them LSD – brought Lilly a lot of fame, but ultimately led to nothing but a tragic end for one of the dolphins at the center of his experiments. For more than a decade after that, the study of dolphin communication was “the punchline of a joke in scientific circles”. says Rendell, but “we’ve had this flowering in the last 15 to 20 years of understanding and knowledge about cetacean society and communication”, which he says has “taken the whole field on to a new level of credibility. And my main fear is that it is being undermined by these irresponsible claims.”

King says it all comes back to testing any AI findings with the experts: the animals themselves. “I think you have to use these AI and machine learning approaches alongside careful examination of the animals: when they produce calls, and in what context, and how they behave,” she says. This is patient, painstaking work that requires careful studies in the field, often conducted over years – the opposite of Silicon Valley’s “move fast and break things” ethos.

  • Dolphins detect sound waves through their lower jaws and produce sounds through the top of their heads. King describes how that works as buzzes made by a nearby dolphin are picked up by underwater microphones. Credit: Amy Martin, Threshold

The days I spent on the water with King involved a lot of quiet waiting, scanning the horizon for the glint of dolphins rising to the surface. When we spotted an animal, King would immediately beginning calling out names – Juicy, Jungle, Piccolo – while the scientists-in-training on the boat with us snapped photographs and took notes. King can identify hundreds of individual dolphins after the briefest glimpse of their dorsal fins, a skill she attributes to the countless hours she has spent in Shark Bay, observing the animals on site. “I come every year, and it’s a really important part of my life,” she says.

She also believes it’s a really important part of doing good science. When they return from the field, her students will spend time looking through the photographs of the fins, matching them to pictures from previous years in their dolphin “look book”. King says lately some students have been asking her to let AI do that work. It would, of course, be much faster. But she insists they do it manually. “If you really want to understand behavior, then the details matter,” she says. “And the details take time. You can’t rush it.”

Meanwhile, a larger question looms for all of us: as exciting as it might be to imagine walking around with an animal translator in our pockets, do we have to wait for new technology to pay more attention to our planetmates? Because whether or not AI ever allows us to talk with animals, there’s nothing stopping us from listening to them, and caring about their lives.

  • Amy Martin is the founder and executive producer of Threshold, a Peabody award-winning documentary podcast. She is now writing her first book

australia.title: Poorer nations will be among the last to benefit if global emissions cut to net zero
australia.snippet: Scientists found unequal impact of the climate crisis would not be reversed even if implicit goal of the 2015 Paris agreement is achieved...
australia.content:
The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the world’s poorest people, including those in tropical areas, has been highlighted by new research that finds they will be among the last to feel the benefits if global greenhouse gas emissions are cut to net zero.

Temperatures have risen more significantly in tropical areas relative to their historic range than at higher latitudes, including in wealthier countries in Europe and North America.

A team of Australian climate scientists found this inequality would not be reversed if global emissions reached net zero – the implicit goal of the landmark 2015 Paris agreement – and could take “many decades to begin to reverse” if carbon dioxide was drawn from the atmosphere under a “net-negative emissions” plan.

The research coincided with the UN’s refugee agency releasing a report showing how the climate crisis was increasing the risk of people becoming stateless.

The climate inequality study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, was led by Dr Andrew King and colleagues at the University of Melbourne. They looked at three sets of computer modelling experiments of the likely temperature changes if global emissions reached net zero and overlaid the results with countries’ gross domestic product.

“If we follow a path that is close to net zero, then the inequality we see in present day warming persists indefinitely,” King said. “The wealthier countries that have caused more of the problem are not those that are the most exposed, even beyond net zero. The regions that have not caused the warming are those that experience the most warming.”

King said the fate of the planet’s poorest regions, which tend to be concentrated closer to the equator, would depend on how much greenhouse gas was emitted before the world reached net zero.

“Even when we get to net zero, we have still emitted an enormous amount of carbon into the atmosphere and its effects will continue for centuries. We can’t easily undo all that damage,” he said. “Getting to net zero sooner means we are less likely to have that long-term warming after net zero. We need to get to net zero sooner to limit that inequality.”

King said tropical ecosystems, such as some coral reefs, had mostly evolved to exist in a narrower temperature range than ecosystems at higher latitudes and would continue to be heavily affected for longer as the world cut emissions.

A separate report on the impact of climate change on the stateless, commissioned by the UN refugee agency and released with the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness, called on nations to support “the continuity of statehood” for countries facing extreme climate damage. It said those at risk included Pacific islands that were losing land to rising seas.

The agency estimated about 4.5 million people were stateless but said it accepted the number was probably much larger as stateless people were “invisible to official statistics”.

The report said the climate crisis risked creating more stateless people through displacement after climate-driven disasters such as fire, flood and sea level rise.

University of Melbourne Associate Prof Radha Govil, a report co-author, said there was a correlation between the regions most affected by climate change and statelessness.

The report recommended countries should be helped to digitise citizenship records, and steps should be taken to ensure children were afforded citizenship if they were left without parents after a disaster.

It said the risks to children were increased if mothers were not given the same rights as fathers to confer their own nationality to their children.

“The recommendations we have set out are absolutely doable,” said Govil. “They can stave of this risk of statelessness and get ahead of this problem.”

australia.title: Australia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong Kong
australia.snippet: Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed Follow our Australia news...
australia.content:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.

Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.

The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.

The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.

“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.

“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.

“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”

Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.

The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.

“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.

While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.

Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.

“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.

Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.

Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.

More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.

Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.

Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.

“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.

“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

australia.title: AI could be a bubble and is not yet making Australia more productive, Michele Bullock says
australia.snippet: RBA governor says AI is ‘great white hope’ but its adoption is so far adding to inflation, rather than economic growth Get our breaking n...
australia.content:
The Reserve Bank governor said AI could be a bubble and there was no evidence it is making the economy more efficient, as the Albanese government claims the technology will solve Australia’s economic malaise.

Ahead of an expected interest rate rise next week Michele Bullock also said the slump in house prices was deeper than others in Australia’s recent history.

Resurgent oil prices and inflation are weighing on markets but US tech stocks surged on Monday after Facebook owner Meta debuted its new Muse AI agent and saw its shares rise 11%.

Bullock said a messy slump in tech values could hurt economic activity, speaking at a CEDA event in Sydney.

“All central banks are a little bit worried about that,” Bullock said.

“Some people think it’s a bubble, some people don’t. I don’t have a particular view one way or the other, but it’s a risk that I think we’re watching.”

Bullock said the RBA and its overseas colleagues believed AI was “the great white hope” to make economies more productive but had seen little sign of any effect yet, with rapid adoption and investment in datacentres adding to inflation instead.

She cited research from the RBA’s South Korean counterpart that found employees adopting AI tended to produce the same output but work 1.5 hours less each week.

“[While] people fiddle around and try and figure out what to do with this new technology, productivity actually can decline,” Bullock said. “But once we reimagine our business processes… then you might see productivity take off.”

The Australian government’s intergenerational report, released on Tuesday, relied on the potential “profound” boost from AI in its projection that Australians’ inflation-adjusted per-person economic activity would rise from $99,200 today to $157,300 by 2066.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, told the Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast: “It’s the most transformative thing that will happen in our lifetime.”

The report assumed productivity would return to its long run level of improving by 1.2% a year, which economists have said appears unlikely. If productivity only rose by 0.8%, per-person activity would only hit $136,600 by 2066.

Bullock said on Tuesday: “Many have put it, ‘well, it’s an unrealistic assumption, we’re not going to get that.’ I guess the way I’m trying to think about it is, ‘OK, that’s what we’ve got to aim at.”

Housing downturn

As the government defends Australia’s easing rate of immigration, Bullock said immigration was almost entirely responsible for Australia’s economic growth in the last year.

Bullock said new arrivals did not add to inflation as they typically worked as well as spending money. She said the exception was the housing market, as new immigrants did not immediately generate new housing supply.

“Where it bites is the housing market, because the housing market can’t respond,” she said.

One Nation has called for more migrants to leave Australia than arrive over three years, including reducing the number of temporary migrants by more than 750,000.

Labor has instead planned to tighten the existing immigration intake, which home affairs minister Tony Burke said would be “part of the solution for the housing crisis” – but Burke warned more severe cuts could “trash the economy”.

House prices have fallen 3.1% over the past three months after the RBA lifted interest rates three times and the government reformed property investor tax breaks. Bullock said home loan approvals had slumped, in her most explicit public comments on the budget to date.

“They’ve dropped for everyone but they’ve really dropped a long way for investors, so it has changed the dynamic for investors, whether it’s worth investing in housing or not,” she said.

Bullock said housing had become “pretty unaffordable” before the decline, which she described as “a slight dip down after a very long run up”.

“The downturn is sort of in the lower range … but it’s certainly not out of the ballpark of the sorts of downturns we’ve seen in the past,” she said.

She declined to say whether she would recommend an interest rate increase next Tuesday. Traders are betting on more than a 90% chance rates will rise from 4.35% to 4.6%, which would be a 14-year high.

australia.title: Jacinda Ardern and husband Clarke Gayford buy $5.3m home in Sydney’s northern beaches
australia.snippet: Former New Zealand prime minister’s purchase is the highest sale price recorded in suburb of Dee Why this year Get our breaking news emai...
australia.content:
Jacinda Ardern and her husband, Clarke Gayford, have bought a $5.3m home in Sydney’s northern beaches, according to a source with knowledge of the sale.

The former New Zealand prime minister settled on a home in Dee Why after looking at properties in the area including in nearby Curl Curl.

The sale – handled by Raine & Horne Northern Beaches and first reported by the Sydney Morning Herald – is the biggest the suburb has recorded this year, according to the source familiar with the transaction.

The Guardian has contacted Gayford and a representative for Ardern for comment.

In February, Ardern’s office confirmed she was living in Australia, following media reports that she, her husband and their daughter, Neve, had attended open home viewings in Sydney’s northern beaches.

“The family has been travelling for a few years now,” a spokesperson from her office told the Guardian at the time.

“For the moment they’re basing themselves out of Australia – they have work there, and it brings the added bonus of more time back home in New Zealand.”

The spokesperson did not elaborate on when the family arrived in Australia nor what kind of work they were doing, but noted it was not unusual for former leaders to spend time overseas after leaving office.

Ardern announced her retirement from politics in January 2023, after five years as New Zealand’s prime minister and the leader of the country’s Labour party.

When she was elected to the top job in October 2017, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, aged 37, and later became the second woman to give birth while holding elected office.

Since leaving office, Ardern has taken up dual fellowship roles at Harvard University, continued her work on the Christchurch Call – a project she established to combat online extremism after the 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings – and joined the board of trustees of Prince William’s Earthshot prize.

New Zealand has been grappling with a surge in the number of citizens leaving the country because of a weak economy, high living costs and high unemployment. Many of these people have moved to Australia.

  • Additional reporting by Eva Corlett

world.title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns
world.snippet: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID ...
world.content:
The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.

The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.

The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.

A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.

The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.

External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.

The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.

Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.

At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.

The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.

“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”

Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.

“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”

The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.

The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.

The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

world.title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals
world.snippet: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is o...
world.content:
Nika’s story

No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.

Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.

Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.

Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.

After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.

“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”

The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?

Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.

It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.

The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.

A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.

A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.


The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.

Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.

Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters

The rug pull

Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.

Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.

Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.

Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.

This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.

Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.

For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.

Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”

Image credit: Guardian Design/AP/Reuters

African deals

When Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.

A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going.”

Kuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.

She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.

In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.

“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”


The drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire to end most migration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.

Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its name incorporating a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.

Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.

They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.

The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.

Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.

On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.

“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.

During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”

Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.

The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”

He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”

Image credit: Guardian Design/Rabbiatu Kuyateh

Malaria

Onboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.

For several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.

Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.

US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.

When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”


Back in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.

The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.

The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”

Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters

As the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.

Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.

In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.

According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.


Nika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”

The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.

An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”

Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.

“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”

Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Alamy

Life in the shadows

People who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”

She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”

She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.

Annan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.

In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.

It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”

Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.

He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.

In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.

Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Rabbiatu Kuyateh

Exhaustion

In Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.

Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”

Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.
